words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Gestur kemur inn úr snjónum. Bjarni þekkir hann ekki: „Hver ert þú?“
Guðrún segir: „Hér er sæti.“ Gesturinn hefur sæti og mat.
Ásta spyr: „Hvar er hann heima?“ Hallur segir ekki hvar. Hér er hann gestur.
words_with_history.note_en: Gestur can mean a guest or an unfamiliar visitor. Here Bjarni hears “stranger”, while Guðrún treats the same man as someone to welcome and feed.

grammar.title: Ég er · þú ert
grammar.rule: Ég er · þú ert · við erum · þið eruð. Ég kalla · við köllum · þið kallið.
grammar.note_en:
A personal pronoun stands for a person or group. Ég means “I”, the speaker; þú means “you” when speaking to one person. Við means “we”, a group including the speaker. Þið means “you” when speaking to two or more people. Hann, hún and það mean “he”, “she” and “it”; þeir, þær and þau mean “they”. First person means the speaker (ég, við), second person the listener (þú, þið), and third person someone or something being discussed. A name is third person: Bjarni takes the same verb as hann.

The present-tense verb changes to match the person and number of its subject. Vera, “be”, is irregular: Ég er gestur (“I am a guest”), Þú ert bóndi (“You are a farmer”), Hér er gestur (“Here is a guest”), Við erum forvitin (“We are curious”), Þið eruð forvitin (“You are curious”, to both children), Við erum öll gestir (“We are all guests”). Compare the earlier Fólkið er inni (“The household is indoors”): fólk is grammatically singular even though it refers to several people. The table gives each form, not a rule for building er from an ending.

Hafa, “have”, is also irregular: Ég hef nafn (“I have a name”), Þú hefur nafn líka (“You have a name too”), Gesturinn hefur eitt nafn (“The guest has one name”), Við höfum nöfn (“We have names”), Þið hafið mörg nöfn (“You have many names”), Þau hafa graut (“They have porridge”). Notice hef after ég, but hefur after þú and a singular third-person subject. The forms höfum and hafið differ both in their vowel and their ending: learn the whole forms.

With regular -ar verbs, remove the final -a of the dictionary form to find the stem: kalla → kall-. Add -a for ég, -ar for þú and singular third person, -um for við, -ið for þið, and -a for plural third person. In the story: Ég kalla ekki (“I do not call”), Þú kallar (“You call”), Ásta kallar (“Ásta calls”), Við köllum líka (“We call too”), Þið kallið (“You call”, plural), Börnin kalla (“The children call”). Before the u in -um, the stem vowel a changes to ö: kall- + -um → köllum. This vowel change is called u-umlaut. It belongs to the við form here; do not spread ö through the whole present tense. Compare the same endings in Ég borða graut (“I eat porridge”), Þú borðar líka (“You eat too”), Við borðum saman (“We eat together”), Þið borðið ekki saman (“You are not eating together”). Borða already has ö in its stem.

In the yes/no question Hafið þið góðan mat, börn? (Do you have good food, children?), the verb precedes the subject. In Hver hefur mat um jólin? (Who has food at Christmas?), hver is the subject and comes before hefur. Compare the supplied question patterns: Hver ert þú? (“Who are you?”), Hafið þið góðan mat, börn? (“Do you have good food, children?”). In a statement the subject may come first: Ég hef nafn (“I have a name”). After another opening phrase it follows the verb: Nú er ég hér (“Now I am here”). In an ordinary present-tense statement, ekki follows the finite verb (the verb form that changes to show person and tense): Ég kalla ekki (“I do not call”). Icelandic uses no extra verb corresponding to English “do” in these examples.

Heim and heima extend the movement/place contrast from inn/inni and út/úti: Hvert fer maðurinn? — Heim (“Where is the man going? — Home”), Hvar er hann heima? (“Where is he at home?”). Úr takes the dative: úr snjónum (“out of the snow”), úr bókinni (“from the book”). Hvaðan asks “where from?”; Hvar asks “where?” and Hvert asks “where to?”.

Two words are for recognition here: minn, mín (“my”), as in askurinn minn (“my bowl”), and allir/öll (“all”), as in Við erum öll gestir (“We are all guests”). Their full patterns come later. The supported command Komdu inn! means “Come in!”; it is not another present-tense person form. Gylfi’s Ég heiti Gangleri (“I am called Gangleri”) is the story’s fixed name formula; the wider pattern of verbs outside the -ar group comes next chapter. The story’s name Alföður is kept in Snorri’s form after heitir; it does not teach a new ordinary noun ending.

Vera að + the dictionary form can describe an action in progress: Við erum að borða graut (“We are eating porridge”), Nú er hann ekki að borða (“Now he is not eating”). Learn vera að as a unit here: the form of vera changes with the subject, but borða stays unchanged. The ordinary present borðar can also describe an action happening now; the longer phrase highlights its progress.

Forvitin has two roles in the dialogue: with Ásta it is feminine singular (“curious”, of one girl); with Við, the mixed pair Ásta and Siggi, it is neuter plural. The spelling happens to be the same, but the agreement is different.
